summary: Defines the codecs and profiles parameters for media types that can contain several formats, such as media container types. They let a receiver tell from the Content-Type alone whether it can play the content, which helps devices with limited resources or bandwidth.

plainLanguage.summary:
Some email and web media types are containers: the type name says what shape the file has, not what is inside it. This RFC adds two optional labels to the Content-Type header so the sender can say what is inside.

The codecs label names the encoders needed to play the content, for example mp4a.40.2 for one kind of AAC audio. The profiles label names the profile of the container itself. With both labels the receiving program can decide straight away whether it can play the file.

questions: how to declare codecs in content-type
what is the codecs parameter in content-type
what is the profiles parameter for mp4
subtitle: Two optional labels on a media Content-Type that say which codecs and profiles are inside a container file.

tldr.problem: Some media types are containers: video/3gpp might hold H.263 video, H.264 video, AMR audio or AAC audio, and the type name alone does not say which. A receiver has to open the file and look inside to find out, which is slow and hard on a small device or a thin link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two MIME parameters. The codecs parameter lists the codecs needed to render the content, as dot-separated elements in a name space that depends on the media type. The profiles parameter lists the profile of the container format as a whole.
tldr.outcome: A receiver can decide from the Content-Type alone whether it can play the content, and can reject it, transcode it, or fetch what it needs. The codecs parameter is retained from RFC 4281 with clarifications, and the profiles parameter is new.

facts.value: audio/3gpp, video/3gpp, audio/3gpp2, video/3gpp2, audio/mp4, video/mp4

today: RFC 6381 is a Proposed Standard from August 2011. It obsoletes RFC 4281 and updates RFC 3839, RFC 4337 and RFC 4393 with references to itself. Nothing has obsoleted it in turn.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
One of the original motivations for MIME was the ability to identify the specific media type of a message part. Due to various factors, it is not always possible from looking at the MIME type and subtype to know which specific media formats are contained in the body part, or which codecs are indicated in order to render the content.

There are several media type and subtype combinations, either currently registered or deployed with registration pending, that contain codecs chosen from a set. In the absence of the parameters described here, it is necessary to examine each media element in order to determine the codecs or other features required to render the content. For example, video/3gpp may contain any of the video formats H.263 Profile 0, H.263 Profile 3, H.264, MPEG-4 Simple Profile, and any of the audio formats AMR, AMR-WB, Extended AMR-WB, AAC or Enhanced aacPlus.

In some cases the specific codecs can be determined by examining the header information of the media content. While this is not as bad as examining the entire content, it still requires specialized knowledge of each format and is resource consumptive.

This ambiguity is a problem for various clients and servers. It presents a significant burden to Multimedia Messaging servers, which must examine the media sent in each message in order to determine which codecs are required to render the content; only then can such a server determine if the content requires transcoding or specialized handling prior to being transmitted to the handset. It also presents a challenge to smart clients on devices with constrained memory, processing power or transmission bandwidth, such as cellular telephones, which often need to determine in advance if they are currently capable of rendering the content contained in a message.

With each bucket type, a receiving agent only knows that it has a container format. It does not even know whether content labelled video/3gpp or video/3gpp2 contains video: it might be audio only, audio and video, or video only.
sections.plainLanguage: The problem is that the type name is a bucket, not a promise. A file called video/3gpp might hold a completely different encoder than the one the receiver supports, and the only way to find out today is to open the file and inspect it.

sections.title: What the Codecs Parameter Says
sections.content:
The codecs parameter allows unambiguous specification of all codecs indicated to render the content in the MIME part. It is optional in all current types to which it is added, and future types that contain ambiguity are strongly encouraged to include it.

It applies to files in the family based on the ISO Base Media File Format, and to the QuickTime file format. The media types concerned are audio/3gpp and video/3gpp, audio/3gpp2 and video/3gpp2, audio/mp4, video/mp4 and application/mp4, video/quicktime, and application/mp21. For MPEG-21 files under the type application/mp21, which may but are not required to contain a top-level timed coded resource, the parameter should only be used when that timed material is also present.

The parameter value is a single value, or a comma-separated list of values, identifying the codecs indicated to render the content in the body part. Each value consists of one or more dot-separated elements. The name space for the first element is determined by the MIME type, and the name space for each subsequent element is determined by the preceding element.

When the parameter is used, it must contain all codecs indicated by the content present in the body part, and must not include any codecs that are not indicated by any media element in the body part. Not all indicated codecs are absolutely required in order to render the content, so when a receiver does not support all of them, special handling might be needed: the media elements could be examined to determine whether an unsupported codec is actually required, since there may be alternative tracks such as English and Spanish audio, or timed text that can be dropped.

Although the encoder must create parameter values that are complete and accurate in breadth, receivers must not rely on the parameter values being complete in depth. If a hierarchical rule for a given code was written after a server was implemented, that server would not know what elements to place after it. Although a mismatch is not permitted by this specification, the body part is definitive of the actual codecs needed and the parameter supplied is informative. A receiver that finds codecs in the parameter that no media element indicates should process the body part by discarding the information in the parameter, and the same applies if the parameter does not contain all the indicated codecs.
sections.plainLanguage: The codecs label must list everything the file needs, and must not list anything it does not need. If the label and the file disagree, the file wins, and the receiver is told to ignore the label rather than trust it blindly.

sections.title: Generic Syntax
sections.content:
The codecs parameter takes either of two forms. The first is used when the value does not contain any octets that require encoding. The second uses RFC 2231 to allow arbitrary octets to be encoded. With either form, quotes allow for commas and other characters in tspecials, and quotes may be used even when not required.

The syntax in the RFC uses the BNF rules specified in RFC 2045 and RFC 2231. The simple form is codecs=cod-simple, where the value is either a single identifier or a quoted list of identifiers separated by commas. The fancy form uses the parameter name with an asterisk, codecs*=, followed by an optional charset, a quote, an optional language, another quote, and the encoded identifier list, where each octet that requires encoding is a percent sign followed by two hexadecimal digits. When that form is used, the percent sign, the asterisk and the single quote characters have special meaning and must themselves be percent encoded.

Examples given in the RFC are codecs=a.bb.ccc.d, codecs="a.bb.ccc.d, e.fff", codecs*=''fo%2e and codecs*="''%25%20xz, gork".

While RFC 2231 allows specification of character set and language, this parameter does not contain items intended for human consumption and hence makes no use of language. The language element should be omitted and the character set should also be omitted. A receiver may ignore language and may choose to support only US-ASCII and UTF-8. Implementations must not add comments or folding white space between the tokens except after a comma.
sections.plainLanguage: The value is normally a plain list of names separated by commas. If a name contains characters that are awkward in a header, the RFC 2231 form is used, where the parameter name gains an asterisk and the awkward characters are written as percent escapes.

sections.title: The ISO File Format Name Space
sections.content:
For the ISO Base Media File Format and the QuickTime movie file format, the first element of a codecs parameter value is a sample description entry four-character code as registered by the MP4 Registration Authority. Values are case sensitive.

When the first element is mp4a, indicating some kind of MPEG-4 audio, or mp4v, indicating some kind of MPEG-4 part 2 video, or mp4s, indicating MPEG-4 Systems streams, the second element is the hexadecimal representation of the MP4 Registration Authority ObjectTypeIndication, with the leading "0x" omitted and hence implied. One of the OTI values for mp4a is 40, identifying MPEG-4 audio; for that value the third element identifies the audio ObjectTypeIndication expressed as a decimal number. AAC low complexity has the value 2, so a complete string for AAC-LC would be mp4a.40.2.

One of the OTI values for mp4v is 20, identifying MPEG-4 part 2 video; for that value the third element identifies the video ProfileLevelIndication expressed as a decimal number. MPEG-4 Visual Simple Profile Level 0 has the value 9, so a complete string would be mp4v.20.9.

When the first element is one of the sample entries defined by the Advanced Video Coding specification, such as avc1, avc2, svc1, mvc1 and mvc2, indicating AVC, Scalable Video Coding or Multiview Video Coding, the second element, referred to as avcoti, is the hexadecimal representation of three bytes of the subset sequence parameter set: profile_idc, the byte containing the constraint_set flags, and level_idc. The sample entries avc1 and avc2 do not necessarily indicate that the media contains only AVC NAL units, since the media may be encoded as an SVC or MVC profile; further information is necessary to determine which codec is used.
sections.plainLanguage: For the common container formats the label is built in pieces. The first piece says which sample entry it is, for example mp4a for MPEG-4 audio. The second says which object type it is, in hexadecimal. The third narrows it further, for example the audio object type as a plain number, so that mp4a.40.2 names one specific kind of AAC.

sections.title: The Profiles Parameter
sections.content:
Just as some codecs have a variety of profiles, which are subsets of their functionality within which a bitstream can be coded, some media files can also be profiled and be associated with one or more profile identifiers to which they conform. These profiles can indicate features of the file format itself, which codecs may be present, the profiles of those codecs, and so on. It can be advantageous for a receiving system to know the overall file profiles of a file; under these circumstances it may not be necessary to know the codecs themselves if they are implied by the profile.

The profiles parameter reports on the profile or profiles of the overall container format. A profile of the container format may have restrictions on the features of the container format itself, on what codecs may be included, and on the profiles of those codecs. The profiles parameter does not report directly any profiles of the contained media; when such codec-specific profiles are reported, that report is part of the codecs parameter. The parameter reports only the profiles applying to the complete container.

It applies to Box-structured, also known as atom-structured, files that have an initial box containing compatibility brands, as registered at the MP4 Registration Authority, such as a filetype or segment-type box. A brand can indicate conformance with restrictions regarding which codecs and file format features are used, and adherence to quantitative limits such as the length or size of the file.

For any file format carrying a brand registered at the MP4 Registration Authority, the parameter must list exactly the major brand, followed by the compatible brands, as listed in the filetype box or segment-type box. The major brand must be first, and may be removed from the compatible-brands list. An example might be profiles="mp41,isom,qvXt", indicating that MPEG-4 version 1 is the major brand and preferred use, that the file is compatible with the version of the base file format identified by isom, and that it is also compatible with the specification or profile qvXt.
sections.plainLanguage: The profiles label says which flavour of container the file is. A container profile can restrict which encoders may appear inside it, so a receiver that knows the profile may not even need to read the codecs label.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC lists example Content-Type headers showing the parameter in use. video/3gpp2; codecs="sevc, s263" carries EVRC audio plus H.263 video. audio/3gpp; codecs=samr carries AMR audio. video/3gpp; codecs="s263, samr" carries H.263 video plus AMR audio. audio/3gpp2; codecs=mp4a.E1 carries 13K audio, and video/3gpp2; codecs="mp4v.20.9, mp4a.E1" carries MPEG-4 Visual Simple Profile Level 0 plus 13K voice. video/mp4; codecs="avc1.640028" carries H.264 video, High Profile, Level 4.0. video/mp4; codecs="svc1.56401E, avc1.4D401E" carries SVC video, Scalable High Profile, Level 3.0, with a Main Profile AVC base layer. video/mp4; codecs="mvc1.800030, avc1.640030" carries MVC video, Stereo High Profile, Level 4.2, with a High Profile base layer.

It also notes that it is sometimes helpful to provide additional details for a media element, such as the number of horizontal and vertical pixels or the colour depth. These details are sometimes called media features or media characteristics, and the content-features header provides a way to do so.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the label in use: a single codec, several codecs separated by commas, and the longer forms where the profile and level of an encoder have to be spelled out.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The codecs parameter itself does not alter the security considerations of any of the media types with which it is used. Each audio and video media type has its own set of security considerations that continue to apply, regardless of the use of the parameter.

An incorrect codecs parameter might cause media content to be received by a device that is not capable of rendering it, or might cause media content not to be sent to a device that is capable of receiving it. An incorrect codecs parameter is therefore capable of some types of denial-of-service attacks. However, this is most likely to arise by accident, since an attacker capable of altering media data in transit could cause more harm by altering the media format itself, or even the content type header, rather than just the codecs parameter of the content type header.

To the extent that a receiver reacts to a codecs parameter that indicates an unsupported codec by fetching and installing the required codecs, that reaction needs to be performed carefully and in accord with the system's normal validity and security checks and procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: A wrong label is mostly a nuisance rather than an attack, because anyone able to change it could change the file itself instead. The one thing to be careful about is a receiver that automatically downloads missing decoders on request; that download still has to go through the usual checks.

viz.caption: How the codec names are built up

items.title: mp4a
items.text: MPEG-4 audio. The second element is the object type indication in hexadecimal and the third is the audio object type as a decimal number. AAC low complexity is mp4a.40.2.

items.title: mp4v
items.text: MPEG-4 part 2 video. The second element is the object type indication in hexadecimal and the third is the profile level indication as a decimal number. MPEG-4 Visual Simple Profile Level 0 is mp4v.20.9.

items.title: avc1, avc2, svc1, mvc1, mvc2
items.text: AVC, Scalable Video Coding and Multiview Video Coding. The second element is the profile idc, the constraint set flags byte and the level idc, in hexadecimal. H.264 High Profile Level 4.0 is avc1.640028.

items.title: samr
items.text: AMR audio, used with the 3GPP file formats. A video/3gpp part with codecs="s263, samr" carries H.263 video and AMR audio.

items.title: sevc
items.text: EVRC audio, used with the 3GPP2 file formats. A video/3gpp2 part with codecs="sevc, s263" carries EVRC audio and H.263 video.
